adjudication_label: High-strain-rate flow stress quantification in FeNiCrMn HEA
canonical_question: How does the observed 'higher flow stress' at 10^10 s^-1 compare quantitatively to the baseline at 10^8 s^-1 in Figure 9?

question_variants.question: How does the observed 'higher flow stress' at 10^10 s^-1 compare quantitatively to the baseline at 10^8 s^-1 in Figure 9?
question_variants.resolution_summary: The paper states that higher strain rates correspond to instantaneous dislocation density strengthening which leads to higher flow stress, but it does not provide specific quantitative values comparing 10^10 s^-1 to 10^8 s^-1 in the text, only noting that yield strength was relatively insensitive to strain rate.

answers.answer: Higher strain rates correspond to instantaneous dislocation density strengthening, leading to higher flow stress, but the yield strength was relatively insensitive to strain rate within the simulated range.
answers.measurement_outcome: Higher flow stress at higher strain rates; relatively insensitive yield strength
answers.boundary_limitation: Yield strength relatively insensitive to strain rate within the simulated range.
evidence_spans: The primary dislocations observed were Shockley partial dislocations and stair-rod immobile dislocations.
No BCC atoms were observed in any of the three orientations, indicating that no FCC-to-BCC phase transformation occurred during tensile deformation.
The yield strength of the alloy was relatively insensitive to strain rate within the simulated range.

source_evidence_spans: Higher strain rates correspond to instantaneous dislocation density strengthening, which leads to higher flow stress [ [32] ], as shown in Figure 9 .
